item.title: Wavelet covariances under fixed finite observations: dilation symmetry breaking and distinct endpoint limits
item.description: arXiv:2610.28665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a centered homogeneous generalized Gaussian field with spectral weight $C|\omega|^{-\gamma}$, we prove two-endpoint recovery of normalized posterior wavelet covariances under fixed finite admissible observations. Global dilation symmetry holds if and only if all observation functions vanish. The nonzero wavelet and the observation functions are real Schwartz functions with $M\geq1$ vanishing moments, with $C>0$ and $\gamma<2M+1$. Noise is Gaussian and field-independent, and total observation covariance is positive definite. Under simultaneous dilation of target scales and positions, multiplication by $\lambda^{-\gamma}$ recovers the prior covariance as $\lambda\downarrow0$ and $\lambda\uparrow\infty$, uniformly on every fixed compact target set. If a nonzero observation function exists, additional finite first nonzero Fourier orders $m_\psi,m_i$ at zero of the wavelet and nonzero observation functions yield compact-uniform recovery bounds $O(\lambda^{2m_\psi+1-\gamma})$ and $O(\lambda^{-(2\min_i m_i+1-\gamma)})$, with leading coefficients and cancellation-dependent improvements. The bounds are exact leading orders when their coefficients are nonzero. For the Mat\'ern-type spectrum $S(\omega)=C(\kappa^2+\omega^2)^{-p}$, $\kappa>0$, $1/2<p<M+1/2$, fixed finite noisy point observations yield distinct compact-uniform limits: the homogeneous $C|\omega|^{-2p}$ kernel after multiplication by $\lambda^{-2p}$ at small scales, and the constant-spectrum $S(0)$ kernel without normalization at large scales. A projection-norm criterion treats fixed closed observation subspaces; Mexican-hat formulas illustrate the finite-observation results.
item.dc:creator: Jun Tsuzurugi

item.title: A Duality of the F Distribution
item.description: arXiv:2610.28690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The F distribution arises naturally in linear regression or analysis of variance. Elementary textbooks state the result in terms of the standard normal random vector and fixed projection matrices. More advanced textbooks and research articles have extended the result to spherically symmetric random vectors. We complement the literature with a dual result that the F distribution arises with a fixed vector and random projection matrices generated by a left-spherical random matrix.
item.dc:creator: Zifeng Zhang, Peng Ding, Wen Zhou, Chenlu Shi

item.title: Boot-AVT: Asymptotically Anytime-Valid Testing with Degenerate U-Statistics via Bootstrap
item.description: arXiv:2610.28931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many nonparametric tests are based on $U$-statistics that are degenerate under the null hypothesis. We develop Boot-AVT, a bootstrap procedure for asymptotically anytime-valid testing with these statistics. Using Brownian scaling and time inversion for the limiting Gaussian chaos process, we show that logarithmically penalized maxima over observed and future sample sizes have a common limiting null distribution. A quadratic multiplier bootstrap estimates the corresponding critical values. We also develop Boot-AVT-Multi for joint testing with multiple kernels. For both procedures, we establish uniform consistency of the bootstrap critical values, explicit bounds on size distortion, and asymptotic size $\alpha$ over an unbounded monitoring horizon as the monitoring start tends to infinity. Under fixed alternatives, we derive finite-horizon power bounds and establish power one with finite expected stopping times. Simulation studies evaluate finite-sample size and power in goodness-of-fit, two-sample and independence testing, and real-data analyses compare stopping times.
item.dc:creator: Jixuan Liu, Long Feng, Liuhua Peng, Zhaojun Wang

item.title: Third and Fourth Moment Phenomena for Monochromatic Edges and Applications to Graph-Based Two-Sample Tests
item.description: arXiv:2610.29215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a graph sequence $\{G_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$, denote by $T_n$ the number of monochromatic edges when the vertices of $G_n$ are independently colored red or blue with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$, respectively. We characterize the asymptotic normality of $T_n$, after centering and scaling to unit variance, in terms of subgraph (motif) counts and standardized moments. One of the highlights of our results is a {\it third moment phenomenon}: for every fixed $p\in(0,1)\backslash\{\frac12\}$, asymptotic normality holds if and only if the standardized third moment converges to zero. The more familiar {\it fourth moment condition}, which requires the standardized fourth moment to converge to $3$, gives an equivalent characterization except at the two exceptional probabilities $p=\frac{1\pm1/\sqrt3}{2}$. At these values, the standardized fourth moment converges to $3$ for every graph sequence with a diverging number of edges, even when Gaussian convergence fails. In contrast, in the balanced case $p=\frac12$, the fourth moment condition characterizes asymptotic normality, while the third moment condition is insufficient. These results identify three distinct regimes for moment characterizations of Gaussian convergence, determined by the coloring probability. We further show that the third moment condition remains sufficient in the sparse regime, where $p=p_n \to 0$. As an application, we derive the limiting null distribution of two-sample statistics based on undirected $K$-nearest-neighbor graphs in the Poissonized setting, identifying sharp growth conditions on $K$ for asymptotic normality.
item.dc:creator: Siva Athreya, Bhaswar B. Bhattacharya, Yogesh Dahiya, Karambir Das, Spandan Ghoshal, Sourish Maniyar, Elizabeth Sara Roy

item.title: Time-Uniform Dependent Central Limit Theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.29288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a near-optimal almost sure invariance principle for nonstationary time series under the functional dependence measure (FDM) framework. This result yields a universal time-uniform dependent central limit theorem, which serves as the basis for anytime-valid inference. In particular, we instantiate the theorem through asymptotic confidence sequences (AsympCSs), time-uniform counterparts of asymptotic confidence intervals obtained via central limit theorems, extending those originally proposed in Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) to time series with serial dependence. We further refine their definition because, as we show, it can admit AsympCSs that fail to achieve the desired asymptotic time-uniform coverage for a broad class of data-generating processes, including independent and identically distributed cases. We address this issue by adding a simple eventual-inclusion condition, which in turn permits more flexible variance estimation, particularly useful in time-series settings. For feasible implementation of AsympCSs, we establish strong consistency of HAC variance estimators under the FDM framework, accommodating a wider range of commonly used bandwidth choices than existing results under mixing conditions. As illustrations, we construct AsympCSs for algorithms with Markovian structure and time-series-based causal estimands.
item.dc:creator: Mingxuan Ge, Yanlong Liu

item.title: Minimax Rates for imperfect Physics-Informed Regression
item.description: arXiv:2610.29532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed machine learning incorporates physical knowledge into data-driven models, often through a partial differential equation (PDE) that the target is assumed to satisfy. However, how much this knowledge improves statistical performance remains unclear, especially when the physical model is imperfect. Since satisfying a PDE implies being differentiable, a natural benchmark for physics-informed regression is the best achievable performance when smoothness is the only prior information about the target function. We show that there is a characteristic threshold for the modeling error above which the physical prior cannot improve the convergence rate. The form of this threshold is common to every linear PDE and certain nonlinear PDEs. Below it, the gain depends on the equation type. For classes of elliptic and hyperbolic PDEs with constant coefficients, we establish convergence rates that improve continuously as the modeling error decreases, and prove their minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors. With exact physics, the rates correspond to learning in dimension d-1 rather than d, reflecting the freedom left by unknown boundary or initial data. We also give conditions for computing the estimator with near-linear complexity and show how to tune its hyperparameters without knowing the modeling error.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Doum\`eche (LPSM)

item.title: Optimally Emulating Smooth Functions for Bayesian Analyses
item.description: arXiv:2610.29685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For Bayesian analyses aimed at constraining the parameter space of computationally expensive models by comparison with heterogeneous data sets, model emulators play a pivotal role. Model emulators enable searches through high-dimensional parameter spaces, searches which might otherwise require millions of full model runs. Here, an emulation strategy is presented based on the assumption that the model output can be well described by a polynomial expansion with all terms being independent of one another and with higher order terms being given decreasing weights according to a convergence parameter. It is found that if the expansion's form is constrained to being invariant to rotation and translation of the parameter space that the polynomial form becomes equivalent to that of a Gaussian process emulator using a correlation kernel with a Gaussian form. In the limit that the function is smooth, quantified by a convergence parameter, $\Lambda$, it is found that rather few training points are required to reproduce the full model and provide a good estimate of its uncertainty. An accuracy metric is defined based on an average of the expected uncertainty over the prior before training data are actually gathered. Analytic expressions for the expected accuracy are provided based solely on an expected value of $\Lambda$ and the location of the training points. This enables a tenable optimized placement of training points, which is shown to be significantly superior to random placement or that from Latin hyper-cube sampling. Examples of optimized placement are provided, and the accuracy is studied as a function of various variables, such as the number of model parameters, the number of training points, and the convergence parameter.
item.dc:creator: Scott Pratt, Oleh Savchuk, Eren Erdogan, Ekaksh Kataria, Christal Martin, Syed Afrid Jahan, Frederi Viens

item.title: Existence of Minimizers for the Gaussian Mumford-Shah Model via Covariance Floors on the Value Distribution
item.description: arXiv:2610.29949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Gaussian Mumford-Shah model segments an image into regions by minimizing a continuous multivariate Gaussian negative log-likelihood term plus a perimeter penalty. It is used for scalar- and vector-valued images, in particular hyperspectral images, but the existence of a minimizer in general is not guaranteed. The energy is unbounded below whenever the covariance of a single region degenerates, regardless of the perimeter of the regions. A quantitative covariance floor on the covariances of all regions, or equivalently uniform H\"older continuity with exponent at most one of all one-dimensional marginals of the histogram, guarantees a lower bound on the energy and the existence of a minimizer. Our approach therefore shows that existence follows from a property of the histogram of the image, and we furthermore argue that scale-independent covariance floors cannot exist. Admitting a quantitative covariance floor is generic: it holds almost surely for all images with suitable noise. As applications of our theory, we show the convergence of regularized models used in practice and of numerical methods.
item.dc:creator: Faian Conrad

item.title: When Standardization Spreads Factor Variation Across the Spectrum
item.description: arXiv:2610.30082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standardizing variables by their sample standard deviations is routine in multivariate analysis and removes marginal scale differences before dependence is assessed. The resulting correlation matrix captures both dominant common components and dependence beyond them. A central inferential difficulty arises because the same random sample variances normalize the entire spectrum. In spiked covariance models, the sampling errors of leading and residual eigenvalues can become asymptotically independent. Sample standardization fundamentally changes this behavior and can preserve their dependence, allowing strong factors to remain a major source of uncertainty even after the leading eigenvalues are excluded. To obtain valid inference for both residual and full spectrum statistics, we establish their joint sampling law for sample correlation matrices with diverging spikes. The theory reveals exact trace compensation and statistic dependent transitions between asymptotic independence and dependence as the spikes grow. It leads to tests of an identity correlation matrix under strong factors and a feasible two sample comparison of residual spectral concentration. A sex balanced HapMap analysis illustrates the substantial effect of factor variation on residual spectrum inference.
item.dc:creator: Tanyang Zhou, Yanqing Yin

item.title: Minimax Optimality of the NPMLE for Gaussian Mixtures in Hellinger Distance
item.description: arXiv:2610.30109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze the problem of estimating univariate Gaussian mixture densities using the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) based on $n$ independent and identically distributed samples. We show that the unconstrained NPMLE achieves the minimax optimal rate $\log(n)/n$ in squared Hellinger distance, when the true mixing measure is sub-Gaussian. In addition, we show that when the true mixing measure has compact support, the NMPLE constrained to a compact interval also achieves the minimax optimal rate, which is slightly faster and of order $\log(n)/(n \log \log n)$. Our proof consists of sharply characterizing the local Hellinger bracketing entropy of the class of finite Gaussian mixtures. One of our key technical innovations is to sharply bound the $L^2$ bracketing entropy of balls of bounded-degree polynomials, which may be of independent interest. As an application, we establish the regret-optimality of $g$-modeling procedures based on the NPMLE in the Gaussian Empirical Bayes problem with bounded priors.
item.dc:creator: Shayan Hundrieser, Tudor Manole

item.title: Combining e-values using demi-supermartingales
item.description: arXiv:2603.10329v4 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a new method for combining e-variables through demi-supermartingales, which settles an old conjecture in the literature on nonparametric mean testing. It also provides an explicit concentration bound for a certain Kullback--Leibler-type statistic arising in the stochastic multi-armed bandit literature. All of these combination results hold for independent e-variables as well as for the class of co-valid e-variables, whose dependence structure lies somewhere between independence and sequential validity. The results are further generalized to compound e-variables. The proofs proceed by analyzing elementary symmetric polynomials and their behavior as nonnegative demi-supermartingales.
item.dc:creator: Jiahao Ming, Aaditya Ramdas, Yi Shen, Ruodu Wang, Ian Waudby-Smith

item.title: Universality of approximate message passing under a fourth-moment tail condition
item.description: arXiv:2610.28971v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove state evolution for approximate message passing (AMP) with rectangular random matrices whose entries are independent, centered, and variance-normalized. The row and column dimensions grow with a ratio that converges to a positive finite limit. The entry laws may differ across coordinates and dimensions, and we assume uniform integrability of the fourth powers of the rescaled entries. For entries sampled independently from a fixed law, a finite fourth moment suffices, with no requirement for higher moments. The nonlinearities are continuously differentiable and globally Lipschitz, with bounded continuous first state derivatives. The signal and noise have independent and identically distributed coordinates with finite moments of all orders, and are independent of each other and of the matrix. At every fixed number of iterations, empirical averages of pseudo-Lipschitz functions of order two converge in probability to the limits specified by Gaussian state evolution. These averages include empirical second moments and products of trajectory coordinates. The proof combines an aggregate bound on third derivatives with randomized Lindeberg replacement and operator-norm truncation, without matching third moments or invoking a non-Gaussian universality theorem. We also show that independence of complementary projected components for every deterministic rank-one constraint pair characterizes Gaussian entries. This identifies the limitation of extending Gaussian conditioning identities to independent non-Gaussian matrices. Finally, a variance-profile example shows that average variance normalization alone does not ensure the homogeneous state evolution limits.
item.dc:creator: Ripunjay Dwivedi, Taejoon Kim

item.title: Optimal R\'enyi and Logarithmic Additive Functional Entropy Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.28999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We characterize the minimax sample complexity of estimating R\'enyi entropy from independent samples on an alphabet of size at most $k$, when the known order $\alpha>1$ may vary with $k$. For every fixed additive accuracy $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and success probability $2/3$, we prove matching bounds with constants independent of $k$ and $\alpha$. For $1<\alpha<\log k$, the rate is $\Theta_\varepsilon(\alpha k^{1-1/\alpha}X_\alpha(k,\varepsilon))$, where a monotone scalar inequality defines $X_\alpha$ at noninteger orders. The bounds remain uniform as the order approaches one or an integer, or grows with the alphabet. Integer orders below $\log k$ have rate $\Theta_\varepsilon(\alpha k^{1-1/\alpha})$; orders at least $\log k$ and min-entropy have rate $\Theta_\varepsilon(k\log k)$. We extend the analysis to logarithms of positive additive functionals. For every fixed continuous $f$ satisfying $f(0)=0$, $f(x)>0$ for $x>0$, and $f(x)\sim ax^r$ at zero, with $a>0$ and $r>1$, estimating $-\beta^{-1}\log\sum_i f(p_i)$ at fixed accuracy, for fixed $\beta>0$, has sample complexity $\Theta(k^{1-1/r})$ for integer $r$ and $\Theta(k/\log k)$ otherwise. A replication reduction preserves the sampling experiment and transfers the rates for powers. Smooth flat functions show that regularity alone does not determine the complexity. The upper bound combines polynomial approximation, Gamma count statistics, and an independent pilot, with a global affine correction near order one. The lower bound uses interpolation to construct positive mean-one priors and controls their distinguishability and entropy separation after normalization. Exact count-variance identities and weighted approximation duality connect the two arguments.
item.dc:creator: Arman Adibi, Piotr Krysta

item.title: A unified approach for estimation of unnormalized models via Stein operators
item.description: arXiv:2610.29510v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we develop a unified framework connecting proper scoring rules and Stein's method for the estimation of unnormalized models. We construct a class of proper scoring rules that encompasses score matching, ratio matching, pseudolikelihood, and noise contrastive estimation. We show that these proper scoring rules naturally induce Stein operators. This connection yields a new construction principle for Stein operators, and enables us to study estimators based on these scoring rules through the geometry associated with the induced Stein operators. Using this geometric perspective, we provide a unified characterization of the asymptotic efficiency of the resulting estimators.
item.dc:creator: Mitsuki Nagai, Keisuke Yano

item.title: Weighted Risk Aggregation under Long-Memory Dependence: Pathwise Fluctuations of Exposure-Weighted Losses
item.description: arXiv:2610.29743v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We model insurance loss in each period as deterministic exposure multiplied by a nonnegative function of a long-memory Gaussian sequence. A weighted law of the iterated logarithm yields the exact almost-sure scale and sharp constant of centered cumulative loss. Loss per unit of cumulative exposure converges almost surely to its mean, with an exact error scale common to all admissible exposure profiles; the sharp constant depends on the exposure exponent. Lognormal and quadratic examples, of Hermite ranks one and two, and a simulation illustrate the results. A known spectral formula expresses the quadratic coefficient through a leading eigenvalue.
item.dc:creator: Elina Moldavskaya

item.title: Asymmetric Likelihood-Free Hypothesis Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.29798v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In likelihood-free hypothesis testing (LFHT), given samples from two unknown distributions $P,Q$ on $[n]$ with $\mathrm{d_{TV}}(P,Q)\geq\varepsilon$, and from a third distribution $D\in\{P,Q\}$, the goal is to identify whether $D=P$ or $D=Q$. We study asymmetric likelihood-free hypothesis testing, where the sample budgets $s_P$ and $s_Q$ for $P$ and $Q$ may differ, and characterize the feasible triples $(s_P,s_Q,s_D)$ up to logarithmic factors. We establish that unequal reference budgets can give a polynomial saving. For instance, for constant separation, $n$ samples from $P$ and $n^{3/4}$ from $Q$ allow testing with $\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$ samples from $D$, whereas both existing baselines---symmetric LFHT and unequal-sample closeness testing---require $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ samples from $D$. We further apply our results to non-adaptive distribution 2-clustering, where the sample allocation among $k$ distributions must be fixed before observing any data. We obtain matching upper and lower bounds for this problem up to logarithmic factors in terms of the domain size, number of distributions, smaller cluster size, and separation, both with one cluster distribution known and with both unknown. Comparing with known bounds for adaptive sample allocation gives a worst-case adaptivity gap of $\widetilde\Theta(k^{1/4})$.
item.dc:creator: Gunjan Kumar, Yash Pote, Jonathan Scarlett

item.title: Self-normalized Bernstein Inequalities for Regenerative Processes and Applications to Learning Without Independence
item.description: arXiv:2610.30119v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove a self-normalized Bernstein inequality for bounded functions of a regenerative process with independent, identically distributed marked cycles of finite mean length. The bound uses observed cycle lengths and retains explicit terms for truncation and the cycle ending after the observation horizon. Selecting a tuning parameter from a finite deterministic collection gives a version of Bernstein inequality where all terms are empirical but one, related to the tails of the regeneration times. We then study this term in many regimes: it turns out that it is of second-order in many cases of interest. This is important for applications in machine learning: we prove generalization error bounds for classification with non-i.i.d., regenerative data. These bounds can be used to define learning objectives: by minimizing the first-order term only in the bound, we define agnostic classifiers that still satisfy oracle inequalities. We also show that the bound on the average deviation provided by our results is minimax-optimal in the sample size and in the expected regeneration time. Finally, we combine the Bernstein inequality with a regenerative strong approximation to obtain a Gaussian approximation using an observable block variance estimator.
item.dc:creator: Imon Banerjee, Pierre Alquier

item.title: Extreme change-point detection
item.description: arXiv:2403.19237v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We examine rules for predicting whether a point in $\mathbb{R}$ generated from a 50-50 mixture of two different probability distributions came from one distribution or the other, given limited (or no) information on the two distributions, and, as clues, one point generated randomly from each of the two distributions. We prove that nearest-neighbor prediction does better than chance when we know the two distributions are Gaussian densities without knowing their parameter values. We conjecture that this result holds for general probability distributions and, furthermore, that the nearest-neighbor rule is optimal in this setting, i.e., no other rule can do better than it if we do not know the distributions or do not know their parameters, or both.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Bleakley (CELESTE, LMO)

item.title: High-dimensional linear regression inference via $\ell^2$ weak convergence
item.description: arXiv:2602.07480v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove weak convergence in a separable Hilbert space for estimators of high-dimensional regression coefficients, which yields asymptotic normality and enables direct use of standard asymptotic tools such as the continuous mapping theorem. The approach permits diverging sparsity with a growing number of small nonzero coefficients, while requiring that only finitely many have moderate magnitude. As applications, we develop a test for finitely many linear hypotheses and, via a Scheff\'{e}-type approach, simultaneous inference for infinitely many linear hypotheses, yielding both a global test and simultaneous confidence bands for the regression function. The limiting distributions are given by weighted sums of independent chi-squared variables, and plug-in critical values achieve asymptotically correct size.
item.dc:creator: Kou Fujimori, Koji Tsukuda

item.title: Vertex misalignment and changepoint localization in network time series
item.description: arXiv:2604.20072v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inference for time series of networks often relies on accurate vertex correspondence between network realizations at different times. In practice, such vertex alignments can be misspecified or unknown. We study the impact of errorful vertex alignment on changepoint localization for dynamic networks through two illustrative models, with the key distinction being whether changepoint information is contained in marginal or joint distributions of the time-varying latent positions. We compare localization techniques ranging from the simple network statistic of average degree to the modern procedure of Euclidean mirrors. Our results demonstrate that understanding the interplay of marginal and joint information in the observed network time series is key to robust network inference.
item.dc:creator: Tianyi Chen, Mohammad Sharifi Kiasari, Avanti Athreya, Sijing Yu, Youngser Park, Carey E Priebe, Vince Lyzinski, Zachary Lubberts

item.title: The maximum distance covariance of bounded random vectors
item.description: arXiv:2306.17067v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A sharp upper bound is obtained for the distance covariance of bounded random vectors in terms of the diameters of their supports alone. The bound is attained for all pairs of support diameter constraints and hence provides the maximum distance covariance subject to constraints of this kind. A normalized measure of dependence is derived by dividing distance covariance by the sharp bound when it is positive. Several properties of the resulting quotient are proved, including domination by distance correlation, invariance under similarities, and subadditivity under sums of independent pairs. The quotient is shown to be nonincreasing under the addition of independent noise, a property not shared by distance correlation. The usual sample distance covariance inherits the sharp bound from the population quantity and the associated normalized statistic is strongly consistent.
item.dc:creator: John \c{C}amk{\i}ran

item.title: Certified Decisions
item.description: arXiv:2502.17830v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hypothesis tests and confidence sets are ubiquitous in empirical research, yet their connection to subsequent decision-making is often unclear. We view statistical inference as pairing recommended decisions with guarantees of their quality---or certificates---and develop a theory of certified decisions. Specifically, we attach P-certificates---upper bounds on loss that hold with probability at least $1-\alpha$---to recommended actions. We prove that it is without loss to limit attention to P-certificates generated by minimax decisions over confidence sets, or what Manski (2021) terms "as-if decisions with a set estimate." We further show that such certificates allow safe adoption decisions for ambiguity-averse downstream decision-makers. A parallel argument applies to E-certified decisions obtained from e-values in settings with unbounded loss. We illustrate this view of statistical inference through an application to economic mobility and one to AI model routing.
item.dc:creator: Isaiah Andrews, Jiafeng Chen

item.title: The dynamic generalized covariance measure for conditional independence testing with nonstationary time series
item.description: arXiv:2504.21647v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Identifying relationships among stochastic processes is a core objective in many fields, such as economics. While the standard toolkit for multivariate time series analysis has many advantages, it can be difficult to capture nonlinear dynamics using linear vector autoregressive models. This difficulty has motivated the development of methods for causal discovery and variable selection for nonlinear time series, which routinely employ tests for conditional independence. In this paper, we introduce the first framework for conditional independence testing that works with a single realization of a nonstationary nonlinear process. The proposed test is designed to have power against alternatives in which the expected conditional covariance is non-zero for at least some times. We also discuss an approach for gaining power against a broader range of alternatives. The key technical ingredients of our framework are time-varying nonlinear regression, estimation of local long-run covariance matrices of products of error processes, and a distribution-uniform strong Gaussian approximation.
item.dc:creator: Michael Wieck-Sosa, Michel F. C. Haddad, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Correlation of divergency: c_delta. Being different in a similar way or not
item.description: arXiv:2510.16717v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Matched sets may have unlike mean scores and spreads yet share the same way in which some scores stand apart. Mean gaps and raw-score correlations do not answer this question. Correlation of divergency, c_delta, is put forward to fill that gap. For every score in each of two equally sized, matched sets, it finds how far that score lies from every other score in its own set. It then draws these gaps into one divergence score through a power mean. The Pearson correlation between the two lists of divergence scores is c_delta, which lies between -1 and 1. A high positive value means that the same people or things stand out in both sets, no matter which way their raw scores point. A negative value means that a score far from the rest in one set tends to be matched with a score near the rest in the other, whilst a value near zero shows little linear link. As c_delta stems from within-set gaps, it is unchanged by shifts in overall level or units. It can show whether the same people feel sharply shut out in matched neighbourhood sets, whether the same bacterial strains grow oddly under two drugs, or whether the same proteins stand out in two drug-binding fingerprints. It should sit alongside means and raw-score correlations rather than take their place: c_delta does not show whether an outlier is high or low, nor why it arose. The power p sets the weight given to wide gaps. With p=1 it uses Gini distance, and with p=2 root-mean-square distance. Higher p gives more weight to the furthest gaps but cuts Kish's effective sample size. The raw scores and the choice of p must therefore be read with care.
item.dc:creator: Johan F. Hoorn, Johnny K. W. Ho

item.title: Generalization and Scaling Laws for Mixture-of-Experts Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2604.09175v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a theory of generalization and scaling for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformers that cleanly separates \emph{active} per-input capacity from routing combinatorics. By conditioning on fixed routing patterns and union-bounding across them, we derive a sup-norm covering-number bound whose metric entropy scales with the active parameter budget and incurs a MoE-specific routing overhead. Combined with a standard ERM analysis for squared loss, this yields a generalization bound under a $d$-dimensional manifold data model and $C^\beta$ targets, showing that approximation and estimation trade off as in dense networks once active parameters are accounted for appropriately. We further prove a constructive approximation theorem for MoE architectures, showing that, under the approximation construction, error can decrease either by scaling active capacity or by increasing the number of experts, depending on the dominant bottleneck. From these results we derive neural scaling laws for model size, data size, and compute-optimal tradeoffs. Overall, our results provide a transparent statistical reference point for reasoning about MoE scaling, clarifying which behaviors are certified by worst-case theory and which must arise from data-dependent routing structure or optimization dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Mansour Zoubeirou a Mayaki

item.title: Model-agnostic information transfer and fusion for classification with label noise
item.description: arXiv:2604.25845v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Label noise presents a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning, especially when large-scale datasets are generated via automated processes. An increasingly common and important data paradigm, particularly in domains like medical imaging, involves learning from a large dataset with coarse, noisy labels supplemented by a small, expert-verified, clean dataset. This setting constitutes a typical information transfer and fusion problem. However, the significant distribution shift between the noisy and clean data violates the core overall parametric similarity assumptions of existing statistical transfer learning methods, while their reliance on parametric models is ill-suited for complex data like images. To address these limitations, this paper develops a generic model-agnostic nonparametric framework for classification with label noise, which applies to a broad class of classifiers. Our approach leverages the small clean dataset to ``purify'' the large noisy one and carefully manages the remaining ambiguous samples. This framework is underpinned by a rigorous statistical theory. Its empirical performance is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world application to medical image analysis for pneumonia diagnosis.
item.dc:creator: Zhu Guojun, Zhang Sanguo, Ren Mingyang

item.title: Adaptive auditing of AI systems with anytime-valid guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2605.07002v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A major bottleneck in characterizing the failure modes of generative AI systems is the cost and time of annotation and evaluation. Consequently, adaptive testing paradigms have gained popularity, where one opportunistically decides which cases and how many to annotate based on past results. While this framework is highly practical, its extreme flexibility makes it difficult to draw statistically rigorous conclusions, as it violates classical assumptions: the number of observations is typically limited (often 10 to 50 cases) and decisions regarding sampling and stopping are made in the midst of data collection rather than based a pre-specified rule. To characterize what statistical inferences can be drawn from highly adaptive audits, we introduce a hypothesis testing framework from two "dueling" perspectives: (i) the model's null that asserts there is no failure mode with performance below a target threshold versus (ii) the auditor's null that asserts they have a sampling strategy that will uncover a failure mode. Leveraging Safe Anytime-Valid Inference (SAVI), we formalize the auditor as conducting "testing by betting," which translates into simultaneous e-processes for testing the dueling null hypotheses. Furthermore, if the auditor is sufficiently powerful, we prove that these two hypotheses are asymptotically inverses of each other, in that passage of such an audit certifies the AI system as being globally robust. Empirically, we demonstrate that our proposed testing procedures maintain anytime-valid Type-I error control, outperform pre-specified testing methods, and can reach statistically rigorous conclusions sometimes with as few as 20 observations.
item.dc:creator: Siyu Zhou, Patrick Vossler, Venkatesh Sivaraman, Yifan Mai, Jean Feng

item.title: The Sample Complexity of Multiple Change Point Identification under Bandit Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2605.13252v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study multiple change point localization under bandit feedback. An unknown piecewise-constant function on a compact interval can be queried sequentially at adaptively chosen inputs, and each query returns a noisy evaluation of the function. The goal is to identify a prescribed number of discontinuities, known as change points, within a target precision $\eta$ and confidence level $1-\delta$, while using as few samples as possible. We propose an adaptive algorithm that first detects intervals likely to contain change points and then refines their locations to precision $\eta$. We establish non-asymptotic upper bounds on its sample budget, together with corresponding lower bounds. Prior work shows that jump magnitudes alone determine the asymptotic sample complexity as $\delta\to 0$. We reveal that this picture is incomplete beyond this regime. We demonstrate, both empirically and theoretically, that for general $\delta$ and $\eta$, the complexity is jointly governed by the jumps and the relative positions of the change points.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Graf, Victor Thuot

item.title: Generalised Robust Bayes for Joint Inference of Model and Contamination
item.description: arXiv:2607.25665v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robust generalised Bayesian methods protect parameter inference from contamination but do not generally infer its proportion or identify individual outliers. We propose H\"older--Bayes, which applies the H\"older divergence to a scaled model to construct a joint generalised posterior over model parameters and the contamination proportion, without specifying an outlier distribution. Each posterior draw flags a corresponding number of observations least compatible with the fitted model; averaging selections propagates joint uncertainty to outlier-detection scores. Under fixed, non-negligible contamination, we establish uniform boundedness of the posterior influence function, a finite-sample $n^{-1/2}$ bound on posterior-averaged excess risk, and a Bernstein--von Mises theorem. Tail overlap between the outlier distribution and the fitted model controls the population risk minimiser's bias and the associated change in limiting posterior covariance. Interpreting the posterior temperature as an affine volume scaling yields a closed-form, data-driven choice. Simulations and real-data experiments demonstrate robust estimation, contamination-proportion recovery, and posterior-guided data cleaning.
item.dc:creator: Masahiro Fujisawa, Masaki Adachi, Takuo Matsubara

item.title: Optimal concentration and gradient sensing by perfect monitors
item.description: arXiv:2608.08816v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cells often estimate chemical concentrations from only a few diffusing molecules, whose stochastic motion limits sensing precision. We consider a perfect monitoring instrument that records the instantaneous molecular density throughout a finite region without perturbing the concentration field or distinguishing molecular identities. The standard Berg-Purcell estimator weights all positions uniformly. Here we derive the optimal spatial weighting within a large class of unbiased estimators for both concentration and gradient sensing. Variance minimization maps to an electrostatic problem. Surprisingly, although the instrument monitors the entire volume, the optimal estimator assigns all weight to its boundary, reducing the uncertainty in both concentration and gradient sensing. We extend the results to arbitrary geometries and spatial dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Farshid Jafarpour

item.title: DisCo Algebra: Why Disintegration and Combination Are Not Inverses
item.description: arXiv:2610.15006v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present DisCo algebra---a compositional framework for joint probability built from a symmetric cooperad (disintegration) and a magma-operad (non-associative partial combination, restricted to the image of disintegration) on the bare family $\mathcal{P}_n=\mathrm{Prob}([0,1]^n)$. No probability integral transform, no external summary functions, no enrichment of objects with conditional kernels. The disintegration side uses block-wise joint CDFs as intrinsic, measure-determined 1D summaries, yielding a lossy compression. The combination side reads the same summaries and reconstructs via regular conditional measures, yielding a lossless embedding on admissible inputs. We prove that combination followed by disintegration is the identity on admissible inputs, but disintegration followed by combination is not---it defines a renormalization operator $R_{\mathcal{I}}=\text{Combine}\circ\text{Disintegrate}$. The information loss of this operator is exactly the probability curvature $\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{I}}(\mu)$---the conditional KL divergence between the true conditional distribution and the conditionally independent product. This curvature measures the obstruction to lossless decomposition and reveals a hard limit on how much cross-block dependence can be captured by CDF-based scalar block summaries.
item.dc:creator: Xuexing Lu
